title: Buoys Come Loose Again in the Rio Grande, and Laredo's Mayor Calls for a Pause
excerpt: Buoys in the Rio Grande near Webb County came loose after heavy rain for the second time since July, prompting Mayor Victor Treviño to call for a pause.
content:
Buoys in the Rio Grande near Webb County have come loose after heavy rainfall for the second time since July, prompting Laredo Mayor Victor Treviño to call for their recovery and a pause on further placement, KGNS reported November 11.

KGNS cameras captured loose buoys in the river following the rainfall. Treviño said the buoys landed on the Mexican side of the river, where water intakes are more exposed.

“We had seen this problem before. And that’s why we had said that we had to have a previous study regarding on how the buoys were going to be placed, what the new measures were going to be. And the studies related to that, we have not had any studies. The buoys were placed again. And here we are with a problem again,” Treviño said.

The buoys are floating barriers placed in the Rio Grande to deter crossings. U.S. Customs and Border Protection told KGNS it has placed 14 miles of a planned 122 miles of “waterborne barriers” in the Laredo sector.

A second failure after July

This is not the first time the barriers have broken free. During flooding in July, 70 to 120 buoys were dislodged and traveled down the river from El Paso to Laredo. At a news conference on November 10, Treviño asked federal officials to come to Laredo and explain the risks the buoys pose to the river, flooding, water flow, water quality, and the water supply Laredo families depend on.

The latest incident adds a new fact to that request: the barriers placed in the Laredo sector itself can also come loose in heavy rain, and when they do, they can end up on the Mexican side of the river, near water intakes there.

Azteca residents raise wall fears

Residents of the Azteca neighborhood also told KGNS they worry a border wall could be built through their community.

Cynthia Treviño, who lives in the neighborhood, said she was on the waitlist for an apartment there for seven years and moved in May with her two sons. “It’s a very scary thought, because I don’t know what’s going to happen to us. Where will we go?” she said. “Some of us can’t do that. Some of us work and live check to check. We need to stay in this housing.”

Kimberly Fritz also spoke about the possibility of a wall. “I really wouldn’t like to have the wall up. You know, hopefully, everybody helps so the wall doesn’t have to be there,” she said.

Mayor Treviño said Laredo has avoided a border wall through negotiation and collaboration, and that the city’s safety record and border monitoring make building a wall unnecessary. He said he plans to continue presenting evidence and working with officials to prevent wall construction in the Azteca area.

What happens next

Treviño is calling for the loose buoys to be recovered and for a pause on further placement until the risks are studied. As of the KGNS report, no federal timeline for recovering the loose buoys had been made public, and no study of the barriers’ effects on the river had been released. Webb Watch 956 will keep following the recovery, the pause request, and any federal response.
